subject: Astronomy & Space
title: AGN Feedback: Black Holes Shaping Galaxies
description: A 60-second lesson on AGN Feedback: Black Holes Shaping Galaxies.

hook.text: Supermassive black holes don't just sit at the center—they control how fast their galaxy can grow.

buildup.text: When a black hole feeds, its jets and radiation heat surrounding gas. Hot gas can't collapse to form new stars.

discovery.text: Observations show a tight link between black hole mass and galaxy size. They grow in lockstep over cosmic time.

twist.text: Without AGN feedback, simulations produce galaxies far too massive and star-rich. Black holes act as cosmic thermostats.

climax.text: This feedback loop means black holes—objects that destroy—also regulate creation across the entire galaxy.

punchline.text: Destroyers and regulators. Black holes decide how big a galaxy gets.

quiz.question: How does AGN feedback affect galaxy growth?
options: Jets and radiation from the black hole heat gas, preventing new stars from forming
The black hole absorbs dark matter that would otherwise fuel star formation
AGN feedback accelerates star formation by compressing nearby gas clouds

details.summary: AGN feedback is the process by which energy from an active supermassive black hole regulates its host galaxy's growth. Jets and radiation heat surrounding gas, suppressing star formation and expelling material.
details.whyItMatters: AGN feedback solves a fundamental puzzle: why don't massive galaxies keep growing? Without it, cosmological simulations produce galaxies far too massive and too blue. It's the thermostat of galaxy evolution.
takeaways: Energy from black holes heats gas and suppresses star formation
Creates a self-regulating cycle of galaxy growth
Explains why massive galaxies are red and dead

faq.question: How does a tiny black hole affect an entire galaxy?
faq.answer: While supermassive black holes are tiny compared to their host galaxies, the energy released by accretion is enormous — it can exceed the gravitational binding energy of the galaxy's gas.

faq.question: What evidence supports AGN feedback?
faq.answer: Observations show cavities blown in hot cluster gas by radio jets, massive outflows of gas from active galaxies, and the tight correlation between black hole mass and galaxy bulge properties (M-sigma relation). Simulations without AGN feedback fail to reproduce the observed galaxy population.
